top.line: A founder's exit is the day someone else buys control: leave then, on terms agreed at the start.
top.para: Control can go long before the shares: a founder with 60% can lose it to the board, another with 14% can keep it. When the strategy is no longer yours, move on. Most founders lose the top job early. Negotiate the exit at the start, the Mourinho clause, and write your number down now.

in-short.line: Seven points, from what an exit is to writing your number down.
in-short.para: The exit is when somebody buys control; control can go before ownership; that is the day to leave; founders want to create; most lose the top job early; negotiate the exit at the start; and write your number down now.

exit.line: Control and ownership part company early.
exit.para: A founder can own most of a company and not call the shots, when investors hold board seats, protective vetoes and a drag-along. The reverse also holds: Meta's founder owns about 13.6% of the shares and 61% of the votes. The exit is the day you stop deciding.

leave.line: Founders want to create; when the strategy is no longer theirs, they should go.
leave.para: Companies move from explorer to villager to town planner, which is often what investors want. Staying costs many brilliant founders their health, their sanity and what they could build next, for a couple more zeros. Open source lets you take your work with you.

evidence.line: Most founders lose the top job early, and acquired people leave.
evidence.para: In Wasserman's study of 212 start-ups, half the founders were no longer CEO by year three and fewer than a quarter led the IPO; four in five were forced out. He framed it as rich versus king. After acquisitions, 33% of acquired workers left within a year.

mourinho.line: The Mourinho clause: his exits were priced before anyone needed them.
mourinho.para: My theory, not his words, is that he plans for impact and an exit. The record shows the pricing: a €20m clause each way at Real Madrid, £19.6m from Manchester United, and a reported €15m clause at Benfica. Sky Sports named the pattern third-season syndrome.

negotiate.line: Agree the trigger, the terms, what you keep, and your number.
negotiate.para: Agree at the start what counts as losing control, that leaving then makes you a good leaver with vesting and a price, and that you keep your name, reputation and open source. Investors who know too much control costs them the founder will price it; sometimes leaving is right for everyone.

number.line: Write the number that would make you happy now, and look back at it later.
number.para: Written while you have nothing, it tells you later that you have probably passed it. Selling a slice is not an exit; selling control is, which links back to how a small slice sets the price.

limits.line: A theory, reported figures, different companies, not legal advice, older data.
limits.para: The Mourinho theory is mine, and his motives are not documented. The Benfica clause is as reported. Some founders should run their company for decades. Leaver terms need a lawyer. Wasserman's data are from 2008.

sources.line: A memo, Wasserman, Meta's proxy, Cooley, MIT Sloan, Ashfords, and Mourinho's record.
sources.para: A voice memo of 20 October 2026; Wasserman in HBR, 2008; Meta's 2025 proxy; Cooley GO on control rights; MIT Sloan on acquired hires; Ashfords on leaver provisions; NBC Sports, AFP, Sky Sports, club statements and press reports on Mourinho; and related articles here.
